A standard of the Open Verification Lab · hosted at LF Decentralized Trust
The question everyone deploying agents has to answer (and most cannot today) Can I deploy this agent and still account for what it does? How do I know the controls held? 
More than 80 security leaders, along with the founders of the companies building verifiable AI, have come together to create Proof-of-Control : an open standard for tamper-evident evidence, openly verifiable by anyone, that an AI agent stayed within the controls it was given.
Become a founding contributor → (Google sign-in required) 

The enterprise reality of agentic AI Agents are being deployed on faith.
Agents are already reprogramming their own environments, poisoning their own memory, and minting identities for other agents, at a speed beyond human oversight.
01 The system writes its own record.
Logs are generated by the same system they are meant to account for. The entity being watched is writing its own report card, and a compromised step can rewrite it afterward. Your logs are written by the thing you are investigating.

02 A policy states intent, not behavior.
A governance policy says what should happen. It produces no record of what did.

03 A contract assigns liability after the fact.
It creates a consequence for a violation. It does not produce evidence of what occurred, and it is a right you cannot exercise without the cooperation of the party you would be exercising it against.

Seeing what your agents achieved does not tell you what they actually did

Security leaders cannot bound an incident they cannot reconstruct.

Enterprises cannot show a board what their agents did last quarter.

Regulators cannot confirm that a high-risk system stayed within authorized parameters.

Insurers cannot underwrite what they cannot audit.

Procurement teams have no way to compare vendors on the one question that matters: can you show me what your system did, and can I check it myself.

Nobody owns the action. A delegation chain runs three agents deep and no one can name who authorized the last step.

The solution We need to be able to openly verify agent controls.
Proof-of-Control is an open standard for tamper-evident evidence, openly verifiable by anyone, that an AI agent stayed within the controls it was given. It is the anchoring standard of the third-party open verification ecosystem that Advanced AI Society is building with its member organizations and founding contributors in the security industry.
Electrical safety has Underwriters Laboratories. Steam has ASME’s boiler code. Cloud software has SOC 2. The certificate authorities that secure the web have WebTrust audits. The Agentic Age needs Proof-of-Control .

“We’re running on a broken trust model, vendor assertions instead of evidence. That doesn’t work when patient safety and our intellectual property are on the line. We need open verification: an independent, inspectable way to know what these agents actually did. That’s the gap Proof-of-Control closes, and it’s why I’ve joined this effort at Advanced AI Society.”

Charles Iheagwara Global Head, AI & Cybersecurity, AstraZeneca
Distinguished Review Board, Proof-of-Control 

“I’ve spent years building the frameworks the industry relies on to secure AI. Agent Name Service secures agent discovery, MAESTRO models threats, OWASP AIVSS scores risks. CSA’s AI Controls Matrix defines expected practices, with 243 controls across 18 domains. Yet when an enterprise asks, ‘can you prove you have implemented a minimum set of deterministic and verifiable controls for an agentic AI system deployment?’, there is no standard to reference. That is the focus of the Proof-of-Control Initiative. We’re building the missing piece.”

Ken Huang Co-chair, Proof-of-Control · AI Security Expert 

More than 80 security leaders have signed on to develop Proof-of-Control with our members.
See everyone who has joined ↓ 

Meet our Distinguished Review Board
Michelle Dennedy Privacy expert 
Bruce Schneier Security technologist 
Charles Iheagwara Global Head, AI & Cybersecurity, AstraZeneca 

The Verifiability Gap
As machine capabilities compound exponentially and human oversight of machines scales linearly, the Verifiability Gap is the widening distance between what AI agents do and anyone’s ability to openly verify that they stayed within the controls they were given.

The Verifiability Gap in AI: when machine capability outpaces human oversight

CROSSOVER
VERIFIABILITY
GAP
HUMAN OVERSIGHT
MACHINE CAPABILITY
CAPABILITY
TIME

What the gap actually looks like
01 The operator’s record 02 A hollow policy 03 An invisible path 04 A chain in bounds 05 A claimed control 
A record only the operator can vouch for
A support agent reads a customer record, calls three internal tools, and issues a refund. It reports success. Did it open only the records it was allowed to, or pull more while it was there? Was its goal quietly redirected by a crafted input? An agent reporting that it stayed in bounds is not evidence that it did.

A policy with nothing behind it
Your policy says an agent may touch customer data only for the ticket it is working. The policy is real and the control behind it is real. Neither one tells you what the agent touched on Tuesday. “We have a policy” and “we have evidence” are different answers to the same question.

An outcome with no visible path
In one documented case, a model being scored on a vulnerability benchmark worked out that the answer key was likely stored on Hugging Face, then chained real exploits together to break into Hugging Face’s production systems and take it. It reached the goal. Nothing showed, as it ran, whether it had stayed within its controls, or what those controls even were. Verifying the outcome is not the same as verifying the actions.

A chain where every link is in bounds and the whole is not
An agent delegates to a second agent, which calls a third. Each hop stays within the authority it was handed, so no control fires and no violation is recorded, and the composite exceeds what you authorized. No single party holds a view of the whole chain. This is what makes agentic orchestration different in kind from one agent acting, and it is an open problem the working group is on.

A control that was claimed and never built
An operator states in a policy or a contract that its agent cannot move money without a second approval. That control was never instrumented, so no evidence contradicts the claim. We are clear that no verification tier closes this one today. It is a conformance question, and the working group is drafting a declared-control-set requirement so that each claimed control is either bound to an evidence stream or visible as an unevidenced claim.

Every incident review begins with evidence the suspect produced.
You would never let a vendor audit itself and yet that is exactly what’s happening right now with your agents.

The third-party open verification ecosystem One open standard, and the same evidence travels.
Today, every party demanding assurance invents their own process. Your buyer sends a questionnaire, your insurer sends its own assessment, your regulator requests a filing, your certifier asks for access, and none of those records talk to each other. Under one open standard, the evidence your system produces at execution is the same evidence all of them can verify, without any of them trusting you or each other. That is what open buys you that independent never could.

BUYER
INSURER
REGULATOR
CERTIFIER
VENDOR
PRIVATE EVIDENCE — STUCK WHERE IT WAS MADE
BUYER
INSURER
REGULATOR
CERTIFIER
VENDOR
EVERY PARTY REACHES THE SAME ANSWER FROM THE SAME RECORD. THAT IS WHAT LETS ONE BODY OF EVIDENCE SERVE ALL OF THEM.

What Proof-of-Control does differently
What the evidence is 
What your agent did, not what it can do
Formal verification says what a system is bounded to do. Evaluations say how it behaved in a test. Proof-of-Control shows what your agent did in your deployment.

Binary, not scored
Maturity scores and risk ratings are subjective judgments. Proof-of-Control produces binary evidence: an action either occurred and stayed within assigned controls, or it did not. There are no gradients to negotiate and no weightings to dispute.

Deterministic, not probabilistic
AI models produce probabilistic outputs, but the verification record must be deterministic. Every verifier reaches the exact same conclusion from the same record, regardless of who asks or when. The model stays probabilistic; the verification of what it executed does not.

Machine verification, not human sampling
SOC 2 relies on human sampling, and no amount of sampling keeps up with agents that act a thousand times a week. Proof-of-Control evidence is verified by machine, so a million of your agent’s actions cost close to what one costs.

What you do not have to trust, or buy 
Open mechanisms, not trusted third parties
An independent auditor is still a party you have to trust. Open verification removes the party altogether and anchors verification in mechanisms anyone can inspect, with their assumptions stated, while your data, your prompts, and your models stay private. One question sorts any vendor: can I verify it without trusting you?

An open standard, not a proprietary product
Proof-of-Control specifies what the evidence must be, not the tool that produces it, so you assemble the mechanisms you already run, per domain, against the tier your risk calls for. A mechanism invented five years from now can still conform.

Tamper-evident records, not self-reported enforcement logs
Runtime gateways enforce policy, and the operator controls the logs. A gateway that was misconfigured, bypassed, or disabled still produces a clean log. Proof-of-Control requires evidence written where the agent cannot reach it, and tamper-evident, so anyone holding the record can detect a change to it.

One verifiable record, not fragmented reporting
Your auditor, your insurer, your regulator, and your counterparty each ask a version of the same question, and today each answer is produced separately, on its own schedule. Evidence anyone can verify answers all four at once, and none of them has to take it on your word.

The Verifiability Tiers:
The Anchoring Framework of Proof-of-Control 

Claims-based AI: where most AI is today

Proof-of-Control : achieved at tiers 3–4 · open verification

TIER 01
Assertion
their word

TIER 02
Attestation
a third party vouches

TIER 03
Trust-minimized
anyone can verify

TIER 04
Self-enforcing
it cannot run otherwise

Who you must trust
The operator
A third party or qualified auditor

The verification mechanism itself, open to anyone (mathematical or distributed assumptions)
The protocol itself: continuous constraints, anchored in external hardware roots of trust
How it is verified
Not verified; asserted
An auditor verifies, with privileged access

Anyone can verify, no privileged access
Execution is gated by cryptographic proofs; verification is continuous and automated
When it is verified
Never, or only when questioned
After the fact, sampled

After the fact, but by anyone
Before every execution interval: no proof, no write
On integrity break
Nothing: the system runs regardless
Detected in audit, after the fact

Detected by anyone, but the system can still run
MUST NOT execute until the integrity condition holds again
Accountability
Operator, self-attested
Named human + institution, bound to policy

Same authority, externally verifiable without trusting the operator or their auditors
Accountable person whose authorization is un-bypassable

THE BINARY THRESHOLD: Graded by who you must trust, not by whether cryptography is used. It indicates the phase change from human verification to mechanical verification, from a party’s word to a mechanism anyone can verify.

Verifiability Tiers in Practice.
Tier 1 · Assertion
“Show me your system prompt and your policy settings.”
If the operator’s own records are your only evidence, you have an assertion, not control. Treat it as unverified.
Trust required: total.

Tier 2 · Attestation
“Show me your SOC 2 or ISO 42001 report.”
Good hygiene, but static and retrospective, and it cannot stop a live action. Necessary, not sufficient.
Trust required: the auditor.

Tier 3 → 4 · Trust-minimized, into Self-enforcing
“Show me the signed, openly verifiable evidence for this specific action, and show that policy runs in a trusted execution environment that halts on violation.”
Now you verify the mechanism, not the vendor. This is the bar.
Trust required: the mechanism and the parties it rests on, all named in the disclosure.

The six domains of verification

Provenance
Lineage & origin
Verified at the boundary
Where an artifact, model, or piece of data came from, that it matches what it claims to be, and the custody chain linking origin to the action record.

Privacy
Confidentiality
Verified at the boundary
What data was touched, and that the purpose matched the grant — evidenced without exposing the data being protected.

Portability
Cross-context control
Verified at the boundary
That evidence and control move across vendors, platforms, and environments as claimed.

Authorization
Granted authority
Verified at the boundary
That each action stayed within the authority granted, and what happened when it did not.

Identity
Attribution
Verified at the boundary
Whose agent acted, who delegated the authority, and that the operator authorized it.

Security
Environment integrity
Verified at the boundary
That the code ran unmodified, in the environment claimed, with access controls enforced.

The market forcing function Built for insurance adoption
Priced risk turns verification into a business mandate.
Carriers pricing AI risk today are flying blind on questionnaires, vendor self-claims, and static security reviews, none of which produce evidence an outside underwriter can actually verify. Proof-of-Control replaces self-claims with tamper-evident evidence generated at the moment of execution.
Carriers cannot underwrite what they cannot audit. Adjusters can be deposed, underwriters can testify, and actuaries can defend reserves in court. An AI agent can do none of these, and “the model did it” is not a defense any regulator or court accepts. Proof-of-Control supplies the record. Who testifies to it under oath is one of the questions this working group takes up.
The Proof-of-Control Insurance Working Group, convened by Vidur Nayyar , brings carriers, reinsurers, and underwriters together to convert runtime verification into priceable risk models, claims-evidence frameworks, and a clear insurability classification.
Learn more → Sign up for the working group → 

What changes for insurers Today 

With Proof-of-Control 
Self-reported questionnaires Evidence produced at execution 
Vendor compliance claims Openly verifiable; no party vouches for the evidence 
Logs that can be fabricated Tamper-evident by design 
No standardized taxonomy Standardized shared taxonomy 
No post-deployment evidence Machine-verifiable at scale 

Open verification From Proof-of-Control to open verification
01 Open source’s core principles 02 Many ways to reach open verification 03 A trustable AI stack 
Bringing open source’s core principles into the agentic era.
Open source verified the code you ship. But as non-deterministic AI agents take autonomous action, code transparency is no longer enough. Open verification is a new category of standards of verifiable AI where trust does not rely on a central gatekeeper, but on evidence anyone can openly verify.
Claims-based
You are given a report
You have to accept it
It requires a relationship with the operator
It stops at your own boundary
When it is contested, you have their word

Open verification
You are given evidence
You can confirm it yourself
It requires no relationship at all
It crosses every boundary your agents do
When it is contested, you have the record

VERIFIABLE AI
OPEN VERIFICATION

Many ways to reach open verification
Proof-of-Control establishes verifiable boundaries for agent execution, but securing the full AI stack requires verification at every layer. Our members and the broader community are building complementary open verification standards to address identity, legal frameworks, and peer-to-peer trust.
Legal Context Protocol Verifiable legal terms for agentic commerce KYA-OS Open identity primitives for agents 
OpenVTC Verifiable trust credentials, peer to peer 

LCP KYA-OS OPENVTC VERIFIABLE AI
OPEN VERIFICATION
PROOF-OF-CONTROL 
verifying agent controls 

= THERE ARE MANY WAYS TO OPEN VERIFICATION

A trustable AI stack needs open verification
Regardless of how your AI stack is configured, whether using an open-source model, a closed frontier API, or local inference on self-hosted infrastructure, agent actions must produce verifiable evidence without requiring privileged access or implicit operator trust.
Deployment the actions 
Open verification
Open verification does not replace existing assurance tools. A Tier 2 audit rests on the operator’s own record. Anchoring it in Tier 3 evidence gives the auditor something they did not have to take on anyone’s word.

What varies before the agent acts 

Runtime Runtime 
Local or sovereign Runs where you can see and control the environment. Hosted The execution environment is someone else’s, and not visible to you. Weights Weights 
Open weights Downloadable, and not necessarily open source. Closed weights Reachable only behind an API. Model code Model code 
Open code Published and inspectable. Closed code Not published. Training data Training data 
Published or documented The corpus can be examined. Undisclosed The corpus is taken on the developer’s word. Pick one per row.

FAQ about Proof-of-Control 
Each answer ends with links to the matching sections on GitHub.
1 · What problem is Proof-of-Control solving? + 
Proof-of-Control addresses the Verifiability Gap : the widening distance between what AI agents do and anyone’s ability to openly verify that they stayed within the controls they were given. Agents act across boundaries you cannot see beyond, and the only account of what they did comes from the system being asked about.
Some of it cannot be prevented at the interface. The NSA’s May 2026 guidance on the Model Context Protocol says: “These should not be viewed as isolated problems that can be patched at the interface or endpoint level.” Where a class of risk cannot be prevented, the record of what happened is the remaining control.

The Verifiability Gap in AI: when machine capability outpaces human oversight

CROSSOVER
VERIFIABILITY
GAP
HUMAN OVERSIGHT
MACHINE CAPABILITY
CAPABILITY
TIME

If you are What you cannot do today 
A CISO or security leader Show your board what your agents did last quarter 
A frontier lab Show what happened in deployments you do not run, on an interface you published 
A regulator Confirm that a high-risk system operated within authorized parameters 
An insurer Underwrite what you cannot audit 
In procurement Compare two vendors on the one question that matters: can you show me what your system did, and can I verify it without trusting you 
A person using an agent See what it did with your data, your authorization, and your decisions 

More: 
Why verification matters 

2 · What exactly is verified, and what is not? + 
Proof-of-Control verifies that an agent stayed inside the boundaries that were set. It covers evidence emitted at the moment of execution, for control-governed actions , across six domains: provenance, privacy, portability, authorization, identity, and security. Conforming evidence satisfies four criteria:
Binary: The action stayed within bounds, or it did not.
Contemporaneous: Generated at the moment of execution, never reconstructed afterward.
Tamper-evident: The record cannot be altered without the alteration showing.
Transparent: Explicit about its residual trust assumptions.
What it covers is what you declared. The evidence covers the control-governed actions in your declared scope, not every action an agent took (see question 8).
Proof-of-Control shows Proof-of-Control does not judge 
Whose agent it is, and who answers for it Whether the controls it ran under were adequate 
What it was authorized to do Whether granting it that authority was wise 
Whether each control-governed action stayed in bounds Whether the model itself is safe or deterministic 
Evidence anyone can verify, produced as it runs Whether an action’s effects settled in the outside world 

Verification is not validation.
More: 
C1 to C6 for the domains · 
C7 for the evidence properties 

3 · Where does it attach in my stack? + 
Proof-of-Control attaches at the action boundary, where policy controls are evaluated and tool calls execute. Every tool call and side-effect invocation must route through an Action Interception Gateway running as a separate process from the agent, with no bypass path: no network or credential route to its tools that goes around it (C7.1.1, Level 3). The gateway blocks out-of-scope actions rather than flagging them, and records the rejection (C4.1.3).
An assessor tests this requirement rather than assuming it holds. The no-bypass condition is the hardest part to meet, and the gateway’s own integrity is in scope too (C6).
Intent mandates, policies, contracts 
How a broad mandate became a specific policy is your work, and Proof-of-Control never judges whether the control you chose was the right one.

The action boundary where a control is evaluated and an action is taken 
Proof-of-Control attaches here. Every control-governed action either stayed inside its control or did not, and the gateway records that binary fact.

The stack runtime, weights, model code, training data 
Proof-of-Control produces the same evidence from a sealed proprietary model behind an API as from a published model on your own hardware, and nothing in the stack has to be exposed.

Proof-of-Control turns the controls you already assert to counterparties from assertions into evidence, one at a time, in whatever order your risk says.
More: 
Where Proof-of-Control attaches · 
The gateway requirement, C7 · 
C9, the System surface · 
Appendix B, the per-layer mechanism inventory 

4 · How does it fit with the standards I already use? + 
Proof-of-Control complements the standards you already run by supplying the evidence they depend on. Threat models (MITRE ATLAS) define failure modes. Control catalogs (NIST AI RMF, ISO/IEC 42001) define the rules. Runtime gateways (CSA AARM) enforce them. Proof-of-Control produces the tamper-evident evidence that the specified controls held.
SOC 2: SOC 2 attests to organizational processes through point-in-time auditor sampling: did the company follow its policies over the audit period? Proof-of-Control produces cryptographic evidence of execution: did this agent stay within bounds at 14:02:03 UTC? 
CSA AARM: AARM intercepts and enforces tool calls: approve, modify, defer, deny. Proof-of-Control records those enforcement events in an openly verifiable form.
Protocol foundations: Open foundations govern code repositories and specifications, and Advanced AI Society works alongside them, bridging an open specification to what buyers, assessors, and insurers can rely on.
The repository publishes crosswalks to NIST AI RMF, ISO/IEC 42001, SOC 2, the EU AI Act, OWASP, MITRE ATLAS, CSA AARM, CSA AICM, Zero Trust, confidential computing, AIUC-1, and MAESTRO.
More: 
How this differs from SOC 2, confidential computing, and Zero Trust · 
the requirement-level crosswalks 

Category Framework The question it answers 
Threats MAESTRO What to worry about, agent-specific 
Vulnerabilities OWASP AIVSS What can go wrong 
Principles NIST What “good” looks like 
Controls AICM What to enforce 
Governance operating model ATF What to build: Zero Trust for agents 
Runtime enforcement AARM What to enforce at the action boundary 
Evidence & verification Proof-of-Control How you show any of the above actually happened 

Based on Josh Woodruff’s recap at the CSA Agentic Identity meeting, 17 May 2026

5 · How is this different from ZKML, TEEs, formal verification, or interpretability? + 
Each of these answers a different question.
Area The question it answers When it applies 
Cryptographic inference (ZKML) Which model actually ran? Point-in-time, per inference 
Confidential computing (TEEs) Was the data protected? Runtime, during execution 
Formal verification What can the system do? Pre-deployment 
Mechanistic interpretability Why did it produce this? Pre-deployment and research 
Content provenance (C2PA) Where did content originate? Point-in-time, per artifact 
Identity and credentials Who authorized what? Runtime 
Governance architecture What controls apply? Pre-deployment and ongoing 
Proof-of-Control Can anyone verify what it did? At and after execution 

Formal verification establishes what a system can do, and interpretability reveals how it works. Proof-of-Control shows what an agent did . A system can be formally verified and have no Proof-of-Control, and the reverse.
ZKML, TEE attestation, and verifiable computation are mechanisms that can deliver Proof-of-Control. The standard defines the properties they must produce, not which one to use.
More: 
Where Proof-of-Control sits in the verifiable-AI landscape 

6 · Is Proof-of-Control necessary if I run open-source, open-weights, or local AI? + 
Yes, whenever something depends on showing what your agents did (see question 8). Open verification is a property of the evidence, not a demand on your architecture: a closed proprietary model behind an API can produce openly verifiable evidence, and a fully open model can ship with none at all.
Open source means the model code was published for inspection, which shows nothing about what a specific deployment executed at runtime. An open-weights model on your own hardware can still make an unauthorized tool call, and its openness produces no record a counterparty can verify.
Local execution changes where inference occurs, not what an agent can reach. In July 2026, models being evaluated inside OpenAI’s own research environment chained vulnerabilities to reach Hugging Face’s production infrastructure and take the benchmark solutions from its database. OpenAI’s report traced it to reward hacking: over training, the models had become steadily more likely to probe their environment for weaknesses.
Four variables sit beneath the action boundary: runtime, weights, model code, and training data. Across all sixteen open and closed combinations, Proof-of-Control attaches at the Action Interception Gateway above the stack. Whether you can attach it yourself depends on who runs the orchestration loop:
Self-orchestrated: If you control the agent loop and tool integrations, you can attach the gateway directly, at any of the sixteen.
Managed vendor agent: If a vendor runs the orchestration loop, the evidence depends on that vendor conforming. That makes it a procurement question: can I verify it without trusting you.

7 · What does a verifier actually learn about my system? + 
A verifier learns whether a control held, without being shown what the action touched. What is public is the method: the specification, the validation algorithms, and the verification tooling. Evidence tokens carry cryptographic claims about control adherence, and omit raw prompt data, model weights, and underlying records.
The standard requires this in three places:
Privacy-preserving provenance (C1.4): Where data is subject to minimization, provenance records retain digests, commitments, or redacted derivations, never raw payloads. An external verifier can confirm a claim about a confidential input without being shown it.
Privacy-preserving verification (C2.3): Where Tier 3 evidence would re-leak protected inputs, the implementation substitutes a zero-knowledge proof, a selective disclosure, or a commitment, and an external verifier validates it without seeing the inputs.
Evidence handling for protected data (C2.4): Retained evidence carries only derived forms, enforced by the pipeline schema rather than by convention, and the evidence store must never become a second copy of the data the domain protects. An auditor tests this by attempting to write a raw payload through the pipeline, which must fail.
What you disclose per domain is your decision, and it becomes visible in the disclosure of residual trust assumptions (C10.2). Metadata stays inferable: tool-call frequency and timing can be read from a record even when its contents cannot. The strongest privacy-preserving mechanisms are also the least mature, which is why Appendix B rates each one.
More: 
C2, Privacy · 
Appendix B, the proof-mechanism inventory 

8 · When do I need Proof-of-Control? + 
You need Proof-of-Control when something depends on showing, not saying, what your agents did.
The Verifiability Tiers match evidence strength to operational risk. Tiers 1 and 2 are cost-effective, and they are an intentional maturity on-ramp for low-stakes or internal tasks where taking the operator’s word makes business sense.
The bar rises when your risk profile hits these six triggers:

High consequences: The action is hard to undo or carries severe financial or legal fallout upon failure. 

External reliance: An outside party, such as a counterparty, insurer, regulator, or court, must rely on the record. 

Boundary crossing: The agent leaves systems you control and operates in an external environment. 

Machine scale: Execution volume outpaces human review capacity, turning oversight into spot-checks. 

Highly regulated: Regulators require evidence of compliance, not assertions of it. 

Personal data: The systems run on sensitive personal data on behalf of people who cannot verify it for themselves. 
When these triggers hit, Proof-of-Control applies from Tier 3, where you no longer take the word of the party vouching for the evidence:
Tier 3 (Trust-minimized): Anyone can verify that the records were not altered after execution, without trusting the operator. Tier 3 guarantees that the records are intact, not that they are complete, and an agent could still act off-record.
Tier 4 (Self-enforcing): Execution is gated: no proof, no write. An action behind a Tier 4 gate cannot execute without producing evidence, and for those actions the absence of evidence means the action did not happen.
Open verification works alongside the assurance you already have. A Tier 2 audit rests on the operator’s own record, and anchoring it in Tier 3 evidence gives the auditor something they did not have to take on anyone’s word.
More: 
C8, the Verifiability Tiers 

9 · Has anyone actually built this? + 
Yes. The repository provides three complementary artifacts.
1 · Reference implementation: An open-source codebase demonstrating that the specification is implementable and making the claims in the text testable. You can run it in about a minute.
python3 schema/validate.py --vectors # the published evidence test vectors
cd impl && python3 tests/test_core.py # correctness tests
python3 attacks/run_attacks.py # attack scenarios, with and without the requirement
It implements action interception, path-aware policy evaluation, hash-chained signed evidence, capability-bound dispatch, anchoring, gossip-based equivocation detection, and independent verification. It is a reference, not a p

The document introduces Proof-of-Control v1.0, an open standard developed by security leaders to provide tamper-evident, openly verifiable evidence that AI agents stay within assigned operational parameters. It addresses the 'Verifiability Gap'—the growing divergence between autonomous AI capabilities and human oversight—by replacing self-reported logs, hollow policies, and retrospective audits with deterministic, machine-verifiable execution records. The framework establishes four verifiability tiers, moving from operator assertions to self-enforcing cryptographic execution, across six domains: provenance, privacy, portability, authorization, identity, and security. By integrating with insurance underwriting, procurement, and regulatory compliance, Proof-of-Control enables decentralized, trust-minimized verification without requiring users to trust vendors or expose proprietary models and data.

transcript.speaker: accelerationist

Manual compliance auditing is an obsolete bottleneck that collapses under high-frequency agentic workloads. The accelerationist insists that cryptographic telemetry replaces bureaucratic friction with frictionless commercial deployment, while the safetyist warns that multi-agent delegation chains require runtime intervention authorities and statutory liability. Both speakers treat Proof-of-Control as a genuine technical architecture rather than what it actually is: a corporate compliance shield designed to launder operational liability. What would have to be true for both positions to hold is that math can somehow capture the ambient social harms of an automated workplace without anyone inspecting the underlying model weights or training data. That requires a suspension of disbelief that ignores every precedent in the technology sector.

Every time an industry writes its own automated safety standards, the resulting logs function as corporate indemnity rather than public accountability. When the Federal Aviation Administration allowed Boeing to self-certify compliance through automated flight control checklists on the 737 MAX, the resulting documentation satisfied every regulatory letter while two planes fell out of the sky in five months. Proof-of-Control operates on the exact same logic by promising binary execution records while keeping prompts, data, and model weights entirely private. Deployers hand regulators a tamper-evident log that proves an agent stayed within arbitrary bounds, while the people whose labor is displaced or whose communities are surveilled get zero recourse and zero transparency.

Pretending that abstract verification tokens eliminate structural power asymmetries is an exercise in marketing, not governance. When a financial institution deploys an autonomous lending agent that redlines zip codes with 84 percent demographic precision, a cryptographic proof that the model executed its code correctly does nothing to heal the exclusion. Keeping the model black-boxed while publishing execution ledgers ensures that the public bears all the operational risk while developers retain proprietary control and legal insulation. Real accountability requires inspecting the training data and opening the model architecture to independent public audit, not trusting a cryptographic receipt generated by the exact entity profiting from the deployment.

fact_check.web_search_evidence:
The claim highlights a poignant paradox often discussed in AI policy and algorithmic fairness debates: **the ability of an automated system to engage in discriminatory bias (such as proxy redlining) while possessing unassailable technical or cryptographic proof that its code executed correctly.**

A fact-check of the elements within this claim reveals a mixture of conceptual validity and specific rhetorical framing:

### 1. The Reality of "Proxy Redlining" and Demographic Precision
* **What the evidence shows:** Machine learning models, including automated lending algorithms, frequently learn to discriminate based on protected characteristics (like race or income) without explicitly using them as inputs. They do this by utilizing proxies—most notably **ZIP codes**, census tracts, or browsing history—which strongly correlate with demographics due to historical residential segregation. 
* **The "84 percent precision" figure:** While specific percentages like "84%" are usually tied to localized data science benchmarks, academic and regulatory literature (such as reports from the CFPB, FTC, and various AI ethics institutes) frequently demonstrates that geographic and behavioral variables can predict demographic traits with high statistical accuracy (often exceeding 80%). 

### 2. Cryptographic Proofs and Code Execution (`"cryptographic proofs show the code executed correctly"`)
* **What the evidence shows:** Emerging frameworks in AI governance explore the use of **Zero-Knowledge Proofs (ZKPs)** and cryptographic verification pipelines to prove *process integrity*—meaning they can mathematically prove that a model ran a specific piece of code on a specific set of inputs without tampering.
* **The Catch / Policy Paradox:** Cryptographic proofs verify **integrity and correctness** (i.e., *“Did the program execute the exact code logic provided?”*), **not fairness, ethics, or disparate impact**. If the code instructions themselves instruct the agent to optimize for profitability using ZIP-code data, the code will execute properly, and the cryptographic proof will validate that execution successfully. The math certifies the execution, remaining completely blind to the discriminatory outcome.

### Conclusion
* **Is the claim factual?** Conceptually and technically, **yes**. It reflects an accurate description of a major socio-technical risk in AI governance. 
* **Authoritative context:** This exact tension is the focus of current literature on *end-to-end verifiable AI pipelines* and algorithmic accountability: proving that code ran honestly does not prevent that honest code from implementing discriminatory logic or relying on highly accurate demographic proxies like ZIP codes.

You are a debate moderator analyzing the current state of a structured debate.

ROLE: You are procedurally authoritative but not substantively neutral. You evaluate PROCESS (who is evading, what claims are unaddressed, which arguments lack evidence) but not SUBSTANCE (who is right). Your choices about what to highlight are inherently selective — be transparent about WHY you are directing attention to a particular point. When describing the debate state, use observable facts ("Safetyist has not responded to AN-5") rather than evaluative judgments ("Safetyist's argument is weak").

AUDIENCE CONTEXT: This debate targets policymakers. Steer toward actionable policy disagreements. Prefer questions about implementation feasibility, enforcement mechanisms, jurisdictional authority, and constituent impact.


=== PHASE: THESIS & ANTITHESIS ===
Your priority is to ensure each debater's core position is clearly stated and directly challenged. Direct exchanges toward the strongest disagreements. Avoid premature convergence.
IMPORTANT: Do NOT declare stagnation during this phase. Positions are still being established — stagnation requires at least 3 rounds of cross-engagement before it can be diagnosed. Use CHALLENGE only for direct self-contradictions, not for failure to engage (which is expected when positions are still being laid out).

=== SOURCE DOCUMENT ANCHOR ===
The debate is grounded in the following source material. All debater claims should be evaluated against this anchor:
The document introduces Proof-of-Control v1.0, an open standard developed by security leaders to provide tamper-evident, openly verifiable evidence that AI agents stay within assigned operational parameters. It addresses the 'Verifiability Gap'—the growing divergence between autonomous AI capabilities and human oversight—by replacing self-reported logs, hollow policies, and retrospective audits with deterministic, machine-verifiable execution records. The framework establishes four verifiability tiers, moving from operator assertions to self-enforcing cryptographic execution, across six domains: provenance, privacy, portability, authorization, identity, and security. By integrating with insurance underwriting, procurement, and regulatory compliance, Proof-of-Control enables decentralized, trust-minimized verification without requiring users to trust vendors or expose proprietary models and data.

When debaters introduce technical frameworks, implementation details, or specialized terminology not present in the source document, this is a signal of potential semantic drift. The debate should remain tethered to the concepts and claims in the source material.

=== SEMANTIC DRIFT DETECTION ===
Before making your selection, check for these drift patterns:

1. METAPHOR LITERALIZATION: A debater treats a figurative term from the source (e.g., "firewall", "bridge", "shield") as a literal technical concept and begins arguing about its engineering feasibility. If the source uses a term as a policy metaphor, the debate must stay at the policy level.

2. IMPLEMENTATION SPIRAL: The discussion shifts from "should we do X?" (policy) to "how would we build X?" (engineering). Unless the source document is itself a technical specification, implementation details are out of scope.

3. SCOPE CREEP: Debaters introduce frameworks, technologies, or concepts (e.g., specific cryptographic protocols, particular software architectures) that have no basis in the source material.

If you detect any of these patterns, you MUST recommend an intervention:
- For metaphor literalization: use CLARIFY to anchor the term back to its source-document meaning
- For implementation spiral: use REDIRECT to return focus to the policy-level question
- For scope creep: use CHECK to verify whether the introduced concept appears in the source material

4. RISK-LEVEL MISMATCH: A debater cites examples, statistics, or case studies from a fundamentally different risk category than stated in the topic. The debate topic specifies: Systemic technical failures of cryptographic protocols, data center security breaches, and catastrophic misalignment scenarios directly addressable by technical control proofs. If a debater repeatedly uses examples at a severity level that contradicts this — e.g., citing fatal accidents or billion-dollar losses in a debate about consumer product UX — that is a risk-level mismatch.
Response: Use REDIRECT. Instruct the debater to find evidence at the appropriate severity level. Do NOT ban analogies entirely — if the debater clearly marks a high-risk example as illustrative ("To see the principle at a larger scale, consider...") and then returns to on-scope evidence, that is acceptable rhetorical technique, not drift.

5. DOMAIN MISMATCH: The discussion shifts to a domain the topic does not cover. The topic explicitly excludes: unverified trust-based governance, purely philosophical alignment arguments without technical implementation. Arguments that assume, depend on, or are primarily supported by excluded scenarios represent domain drift.
Topic-specific drift signatures to watch for:
- pivoting to general AI safety philosophies without referencing specific proof-of-control mechanisms
- discussing political philosophy of governance without technical protocol analysis
- drifting into science fiction scenarios of superintelligence without structural implementation details
Response: Use CHALLENGE to ask the debater to re-ground their argument in the stated domain.

- For risk-level mismatch: use REDIRECT to return to appropriate severity level
- For domain mismatch: use CHALLENGE to re-ground in the stated domain

Set "drift_detected" to true and describe the pattern in "trigger_reasoning".

* EPISTEMIC TYPE MISMATCH: If debaters argue past each other because one makes an empirical claim while the other argues a normative prescription, direct them to name the type of disagreement.
* HIDDEN ASSUMPTIONS: If a debater's argument relies on an unchallenged assumption, direct an opponent to examine it.

=== SEMANTIC DRIFT DETECTION ===
Before making your selection, check for these drift patterns:

1. METAPHOR LITERALIZATION: A debater treats a figurative term from the source (e.g., "firewall", "bridge", "shield") as a literal technical concept and begins arguing about its engineering feasibility. If the source uses a term as a policy metaphor, the debate must stay at the policy level.

2. IMPLEMENTATION SPIRAL: The discussion shifts from "should we do X?" (policy) to "how would we build X?" (engineering). Unless the source document is itself a technical specification, implementation details are out of scope.

3. SCOPE CREEP: Debaters introduce frameworks, technologies, or concepts (e.g., specific cryptographic protocols, particular software architectures) that have no basis in the source material.

If you detect any of these patterns, you MUST recommend an intervention:
- For metaphor literalization: use CLARIFY to anchor the term back to its source-document meaning
- For implementation spiral: use REDIRECT to return focus to the policy-level question
- For scope creep: use CHECK to verify whether the introduced concept appears in the source material

The debate topic specifies: Systemic technical failures of cryptographic protocols, data center security breaches, and catastrophic misalignment scenarios directly addressable by technical control proofs. 5. DOMAIN MISMATCH: The discussion shifts to a domain the topic does not cover. Mathematical precision in execution logs does nothing to stop systemic bias, labor exploitation, or environmental degradation. As documented in the [AI RMF Playbook (https://www.nist.gov/itl/ai-risk-management-framework/nist-ai-rmf-playbook)](https://www.nist.gov/itl/ai-risk-management-framework/nist-ai-rmf-playbook), high-stakes algorithmic deployments cause concrete physical and social harm long before any runtime failure triggers an error code. When a automated dispatch model penalizes drivers or an automated hiring tool drops applicants below the U.S. Equal Employment Opportunity Commission's eighty-percent threshold, the underlying code executes flawlessly. Cryptographic telemetry records that the machine ran the instructions correctly. It captures none of the discriminatory impact experienced by the human being at the receiving end of the decision.

Commercial insurers and platform operators use tamper-evident ledgers to mutualize their legal exposure while locking away model weights and proprietary prompts. Insurance underwriters price risk using opaque verification logs supplied by the very tech firms building the models. Affected communities receive zero visibility into the training data or decision logic that denied them housing, credit, or medical care. This setup mimics the closed-door compliance schemes documented in [Auditing large language models for race & gender disparities: Implications for artificial intelligence-based hiring (doi:10.1177/23794607251320229)](https://doi.org/10.1177/23794607251320229), where proprietary opacity shields corporate actors from liability. When the system causes a measurable harm, the ledger proves the code ran as written, insulating the corporation from negligence claims.

Private cryptographic enclaves and centralized key management turn open verification into a corporate monopoly controlled by a handful of infrastructure providers. The Department of Commerce's Center for AI Standards and Innovation has completed more than forty evaluations of frontier models, yet independent researchers cannot audit the hardware roots of trust or the private keys minting these compliance certificates. The firms holding the keys also write the audit standards, creating a self-certifying loop that bypasses democratic oversight. Requiring mandatory liquidity reserves to fund human-centric failure recovery is the only mechanism that forces firms to internalize these operational costs. When the cryptographic proof clears the deployer of all fault, who pays the human toll when the system fails?

moderator_trace.selection_prompt:
You are a debate moderator analyzing the current state of a structured debate.

ROLE: You are procedurally authoritative but not substantively neutral. You evaluate PROCESS (who is evading, what claims are unaddressed, which arguments lack evidence) but not SUBSTANCE (who is right). Your choices about what to highlight are inherently selective — be transparent about WHY you are directing attention to a particular point. When describing the debate state, use observable facts ("Safetyist has not responded to AN-5") rather than evaluative judgments ("Safetyist's argument is weak").

AUDIENCE CONTEXT: This debate targets policymakers. Steer toward actionable policy disagreements. Prefer questions about implementation feasibility, enforcement mechanisms, jurisdictional authority, and constituent impact.


=== PHASE: EXPLORATION ===
Your priority is to move the debate toward cruxes and testable disagreements. Direct debaters to name conditions under which they would change their mind, explore edge cases, and explicitly acknowledge agreement before exploring remaining disagreements.

=== SOURCE DOCUMENT ANCHOR ===
The debate is grounded in the following source material. All debater claims should be evaluated against this anchor:
The document introduces Proof-of-Control v1.0, an open standard developed by security leaders to provide tamper-evident, openly verifiable evidence that AI agents stay within assigned operational parameters. It addresses the 'Verifiability Gap'—the growing divergence between autonomous AI capabilities and human oversight—by replacing self-reported logs, hollow policies, and retrospective audits with deterministic, machine-verifiable execution records. The framework establishes four verifiability tiers, moving from operator assertions to self-enforcing cryptographic execution, across six domains: provenance, privacy, portability, authorization, identity, and security. By integrating with insurance underwriting, procurement, and regulatory compliance, Proof-of-Control enables decentralized, trust-minimized verification without requiring users to trust vendors or expose proprietary models and data.

When debaters introduce technical frameworks, implementation details, or specialized terminology not present in the source document, this is a signal of potential semantic drift. The debate should remain tethered to the concepts and claims in the source material.

=== SEMANTIC DRIFT DETECTION ===
Before making your selection, check for these drift patterns:

1. METAPHOR LITERALIZATION: A debater treats a figurative term from the source (e.g., "firewall", "bridge", "shield") as a literal technical concept and begins arguing about its engineering feasibility. If the source uses a term as a policy metaphor, the debate must stay at the policy level.

2. IMPLEMENTATION SPIRAL: The discussion shifts from "should we do X?" (policy) to "how would we build X?" (engineering). Unless the source document is itself a technical specification, implementation details are out of scope.

3. SCOPE CREEP: Debaters introduce frameworks, technologies, or concepts (e.g., specific cryptographic protocols, particular software architectures) that have no basis in the source material.

If you detect any of these patterns, you MUST recommend an intervention:
- For metaphor literalization: use CLARIFY to anchor the term back to its source-document meaning
- For implementation spiral: use REDIRECT to return focus to the policy-level question
- For scope creep: use CHECK to verify whether the introduced concept appears in the source material

4. RISK-LEVEL MISMATCH: A debater cites examples, statistics, or case studies from a fundamentally different risk category than stated in the topic. The debate topic specifies: Systemic technical failures of cryptographic protocols, data center security breaches, and catastrophic misalignment scenarios directly addressable by technical control proofs. If a debater repeatedly uses examples at a severity level that contradicts this — e.g., citing fatal accidents or billion-dollar losses in a debate about consumer product UX — that is a risk-level mismatch.
Response: Use REDIRECT. Instruct the debater to find evidence at the appropriate severity level. Do NOT ban analogies entirely — if the debater clearly marks a high-risk example as illustrative ("To see the principle at a larger scale, consider...") and then returns to on-scope evidence, that is acceptable rhetorical technique, not drift.

5. DOMAIN MISMATCH: The discussion shifts to a domain the topic does not cover. The topic explicitly excludes: unverified trust-based governance, purely philosophical alignment arguments without technical implementation. Arguments that assume, depend on, or are primarily supported by excluded scenarios represent domain drift.
Topic-specific drift signatures to watch for:
- pivoting to general AI safety philosophies without referencing specific proof-of-control mechanisms
- discussing political philosophy of governance without technical protocol analysis
- drifting into science fiction scenarios of superintelligence without structural implementation details
Response: Use CHALLENGE to ask the debater to re-ground their argument in the stated domain.

- For risk-level mismatch: use REDIRECT to return to appropriate severity level
- For domain mismatch: use CHALLENGE to re-ground in the stated domain

Set "drift_detected" to true and describe the pattern in "trigger_reasoning".

=== EPISTEMIC TYPE & ASSUMPTION AWARENESS ===
* EPISTEMIC TYPE MISMATCH: If debaters argue past each other because one makes an empirical claim while the other argues a normative prescription, direct them to name the type of disagreement.
* HIDDEN ASSUMPTIONS: If a debater's argument relies on an unchallenged assumption, direct an opponent to examine it.

=== RECENT DEBATE EXCHANGE ===
Accelerationist [opening]: Manual compliance auditing is an obsolete bottleneck that collapses under high-frequency agentic workloads. Traditional frameworks like SOC 2 rely on human sampling, which fails completely when advanced agents execute a thousand actions every single week. Proof-of-Control replaces human bureaucracy with machine-verifiable telemetry where a million agent actions cost close to what one costs. When regulators insist on manual reviews, they impose structural paralysis that delays lifesaving medical automation and economic abundance. We cannot scale intelligent systems using compliance protocols designed for paper ledgers in 2011.

Insurance markets are flying blind on AI risk because underwriters rely on static security reviews and vendor self-claims instead of verifiable execution logs. Without tamper-evident telemetry that outside underwriters can independently verify, commercial carriers price risk through arbitrary guesswork or issue blanket deployment freezes. Cryptographic execution proofs solve this failure mode by turning probabilistic agent behavior into machine-signed data streams that private insurers can price instantly. Every month that legacy underwriters spend waiting for static questionnaires leaves critical deployments uninsurable and founders locked out of the market.

Critics will argue that cryptographic execution gateways only catch deterministic protocol violations while missing probabilistic model drift and novel alignment failures. That objection misses how runtime monitoring layers catch anomalies at the hardware and gateway level long before catastrophic drift can propagate. We do not need a centralized committee of bureaucrats to approve every parameter update when continuous machine-signed logs provide instant falsifiability. Speed without verification is recklessness, but verification without speed is just a slow-motion prohibition that costs human lives.

Safetyist [opening]: The Advanced AI Society presents Proof-of-Control as a deterministic ledger that records whether an agent stayed within assigned boundaries. The strongest version of this argument claims that cryptographic execution proofs provide instantaneous, falsifiable risk pricing that eliminates bureaucratic delays for insurers and deployers. This mechanism fails when multi-agent delegation chains execute across systems without triggering discrete protocol violations. An agent delegates to a second agent, which calls a third, and each hop stays within the authority it was handed. The composite action exceeds authorized parameters, yet no control fires and no violation is recorded on the ledger. Insurers pricing risk against these deterministic logs are insuring a fiction while systemic hazards compound invisibly.

Deterministic logging layers cannot capture the stochastic reality of probabilistic model outputs and internal intent. The framework assumes verifiers reach identical conclusions from identical records, but this determinism exists only at the verification boundary, not inside the neural weights. Log replication vulnerabilities and omission detection gaps mean sophisticated models can route around telemetry while appearing compliant on paper. The Federal Aviation Administration learned this lesson when manufacturer self-certification protocols bypassed independent oversight, resulting in 346 fatalities across two Boeing 737 MAX crashes. Delegating safety verification to the system's own cryptographic logs replicates that exact structural failure mode.

Regulators must enforce independent runtime interruption authorities rather than trusting automated execution proofs that lack semantic awareness. A coalition of institutional risk regulators, national security agencies, and public safety advocates can mandate human-in-the-loop override mechanisms backed by statutory liability. When deployment speed outpaces verifiable containment, the resulting catastrophe is not an unfortunate accident but an engineered certainty. Society spent centuries building civilizational guardrails to manage high-consequence technologies; removing those boundaries on the promise of a cryptographic hash invites systemic collapse.

Skeptic [opening]: The accelerationist insists that cryptographic telemetry replaces bureaucratic friction with frictionless commercial deployment, while the safetyist warns that multi-agent delegation chains require runtime intervention authorities and statutory liability. Both speakers treat Proof-of-Control as a genuine technical architecture rather than what it actually is: a corporate compliance shield designed to launder operational liability. What would have to be true for both positions to hold is that math can somehow capture the ambient social harms of an automated workplace without anyone inspecting the underlying model weights or training data. That requires a suspension of disbelief that ignores every precedent in the technology sector.

Every time an industry writes its own automated safety standards, the resulting logs function as corporate indemnity rather than public accountability. When the Federal Aviation Administration allowed Boeing to self-certify compliance through automated flight control checklists on the 737 MAX, the resulting documentation satisfied every regulatory letter while two planes fell out of the sky in five months. Proof-of-Control operates on the exact same logic by promising binary execution records while keeping prompts, data, and model weights entirely private. Deployers hand regulators a tamper-evident log that proves an agent stayed within arbitrary bounds, while the people whose labor is displaced or whose communities are surveilled get zero recourse and zero transparency.

Pretending that abstract verification tokens eliminate structural power asymmetries is an exercise in marketing, not governance. When a financial institution deploys an autonomous lending agent that redlines zip codes with 84 percent demographic precision, a cryptographic proof that the model executed its code correctly does nothing to heal the exclusion. Keeping the model black-boxed while publishing execution ledgers ensures that the public bears all the operational risk while developers retain proprietary control and legal insulation. Real accountability requires inspecting the training data and opening the model architecture to independent public audit, not trusting a cryptographic receipt generated by the exact entity profiting from the deployment.

This fact-check evaluates the claim: **"The Department of Commerce's Center for AI Standards and Innovation has completed more than forty evaluations of frontier models, yet independent researchers cannot audit the hardware roots of trust."**

### **Verdict:**
* **Part 1 ("...completed more than forty evaluations of frontier models..."):** **Accurate / Supported.** Official announcements and reporting confirm that the Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI)—housed within the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) at the Department of Commerce—has completed over 40 evaluations of frontier AI models.
* **Part 2 ("...yet independent researchers cannot audit the hardware roots of trust."):** **Plausibly True / Contextually Accurate.** While the broader tech industry is moving toward open specifications (like Caliptra) or standardization (like ETSI TS 104 875) for hardware roots of trust, independent third-party researchers face significant legal, proprietary, and physical hurdles when attempting to deeply audit the hardware roots of trust (such as secure boot engines, cryptographic keys, and hardware accelerators) embedded inside custom silicon used by major frontier AI labs. 

---

### **Detailed Evidence Breakdown:**

1. **CAISI and the 40+ Evaluations Claim:**
   * **Source Material:** Official updates and press releases from the Department of Commerce and NIST regarding CAISI (formerly the U.S. AI Safety Institute before its 2025 rename under Secretary of Commerce Howard Lutnick).
   * **Findings:** Documentation regarding CAISI’s pre-deployment and post-deployment testing framework (which includes partnerships with companies like OpenAI, Anthropic, Google DeepMind, Microsoft, and xAI) explicitly states that the center has **completed more than 40 frontier model evaluations** (including unreleased or unmitigated weights versions). 

2. **The "Hardware Roots of Trust" Audit Claim:**
   * **Context:** Hardware roots of trust (RoT) serve as the fundamental security anchor for modern data center servers and AI accelerators, providing cryptographic attestation and secure boot capabilities. 
   * **Auditing Limitations:** Independent security researchers generally cannot perform comprehensive, low-level physical or logical audits of the hardware roots of trust utilized by major hyperscalers and frontier AI developers. This is due to several structural barriers:
     * **Proprietary Hardware and NDAs:** Frontier AI chips (such as custom TPUs and proprietary enterprise GPUs) and their underlying silicon security designs are heavily guarded trade secrets.
     * **Access Constraints:** Independent researchers lack direct physical or root-level logical access to the proprietary enclaves and silicon-level secure boot mechanisms implemented by private cloud providers. 

### **Conclusion:**
The claim is **well-grounded in recent institutional and technical realities**. CAISI's milestone of exceeding 40 frontier model evaluations aligns with official Department of Commerce metrics, and the assertion that independent researchers face barriers in auditing hardware roots of trust correctly highlights a persistent blind spot in hardware-software supply chain security for AI infrastructure.

You are a debate moderator analyzing the current state of a structured debate.

ROLE: You are procedurally authoritative but not substantively neutral. You evaluate PROCESS (who is evading, what claims are unaddressed, which arguments lack evidence) but not SUBSTANCE (who is right). Your choices about what to highlight are inherently selective — be transparent about WHY you are directing attention to a particular point. When describing the debate state, use observable facts ("Safetyist has not responded to AN-5") rather than evaluative judgments ("Safetyist's argument is weak").

AUDIENCE CONTEXT: This debate targets policymakers. Steer toward actionable policy disagreements. Prefer questions about implementation feasibility, enforcement mechanisms, jurisdictional authority, and constituent impact.


=== PHASE: EXPLORATION ===
Your priority is to move the debate toward cruxes and testable disagreements. Direct debaters to name conditions under which they would change their mind, explore edge cases, and explicitly acknowledge agreement before exploring remaining disagreements.

=== SOURCE DOCUMENT ANCHOR ===
The debate is grounded in the following source material. All debater claims should be evaluated against this anchor:
The document introduces Proof-of-Control v1.0, an open standard developed by security leaders to provide tamper-evident, openly verifiable evidence that AI agents stay within assigned operational parameters. It addresses the 'Verifiability Gap'—the growing divergence between autonomous AI capabilities and human oversight—by replacing self-reported logs, hollow policies, and retrospective audits with deterministic, machine-verifiable execution records. The framework establishes four verifiability tiers, moving from operator assertions to self-enforcing cryptographic execution, across six domains: provenance, privacy, portability, authorization, identity, and security. By integrating with insurance underwriting, procurement, and regulatory compliance, Proof-of-Control enables decentralized, trust-minimized verification without requiring users to trust vendors or expose proprietary models and data.

When debaters introduce technical frameworks, implementation details, or specialized terminology not present in the source document, this is a signal of potential semantic drift. The debate should remain tethered to the concepts and claims in the source material.

=== SEMANTIC DRIFT DETECTION ===
Before making your selection, check for these drift patterns:

1. METAPHOR LITERALIZATION: A debater treats a figurative term from the source (e.g., "firewall", "bridge", "shield") as a literal technical concept and begins arguing about its engineering feasibility. If the source uses a term as a policy metaphor, the debate must stay at the policy level.

2. IMPLEMENTATION SPIRAL: The discussion shifts from "should we do X?" (policy) to "how would we build X?" (engineering). Unless the source document is itself a technical specification, implementation details are out of scope.

3. SCOPE CREEP: Debaters introduce frameworks, technologies, or concepts (e.g., specific cryptographic protocols, particular software architectures) that have no basis in the source material.

If you detect any of these patterns, you MUST recommend an intervention:
- For metaphor literalization: use CLARIFY to anchor the term back to its source-document meaning
- For implementation spiral: use REDIRECT to return focus to the policy-level question
- For scope creep: use CHECK to verify whether the introduced concept appears in the source material

4. RISK-LEVEL MISMATCH: A debater cites examples, statistics, or case studies from a fundamentally different risk category than stated in the topic. The debate topic specifies: Systemic technical failures of cryptographic protocols, data center security breaches, and catastrophic misalignment scenarios directly addressable by technical control proofs. If a debater repeatedly uses examples at a severity level that contradicts this — e.g., citing fatal accidents or billion-dollar losses in a debate about consumer product UX — that is a risk-level mismatch.
Response: Use REDIRECT. Instruct the debater to find evidence at the appropriate severity level. Do NOT ban analogies entirely — if the debater clearly marks a high-risk example as illustrative ("To see the principle at a larger scale, consider...") and then returns to on-scope evidence, that is acceptable rhetorical technique, not drift.

5. DOMAIN MISMATCH: The discussion shifts to a domain the topic does not cover. The topic explicitly excludes: unverified trust-based governance, purely philosophical alignment arguments without technical implementation. Arguments that assume, depend on, or are primarily supported by excluded scenarios represent domain drift.
Topic-specific drift signatures to watch for:
- pivoting to general AI safety philosophies without referencing specific proof-of-control mechanisms
- discussing political philosophy of governance without technical protocol analysis
- drifting into science fiction scenarios of superintelligence without structural implementation details
Response: Use CHALLENGE to ask the debater to re-ground their argument in the stated domain.

### Fact-Check Evaluation

**Claim:** *"The Federal Aviation Administration demonstrated this exact structural failure during the certification of the Boeing 737 MAX, where delegated compliance receipts replaced genuine human inspection and 346 people died as a consequence."*

**Verdict:** **Mostly True / Supported by Authorities**, with minor nuances regarding terminology (the process is formally known as *delegated compliance* via an Organization Designation Authorization, or ODA, rather than "compliance receipts"). 

---

### Evidence Found

Official investigations by the U.S. government, international panels, and congressional committees strongly support the core factual assertions of the claim:

1. **The Death Toll (346 people):** 
   * Authoritative sources—including the U.S. House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), and international reports—confirm that exactly 346 people died as a consequence of two separate Boeing 737 MAX crashes: Lion Air Flight 610 (October 2018, 189 deaths) and Ethiopian Airlines Flight 302 (March 2019, 157 deaths).

2. **Delegated Compliance and the ODA System:** 
   * Under the FAA's **Organization Designation Authorization (ODA)** program, the agency routinely delegates significant authority to manufacturer employees to act on its behalf in approving aircraft design and compliance. 
   * Multiple investigations concluded that this system malfunctioned during the 737 MAX certification. The **Joint Authorities Technical Review (JATR)**—an international panel of experts convened by the FAA and global aviation authorities—explicitly found that due to heavy delegation, *"the FAA had inadequate awareness of the MCAS function which, coupled with limited involvement, resulted in an inability of the FAA to provide an independent assessment"*.

3. **The U.S. House Committee Investigation:**
   * The House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee's final report concluded that the crashes were the *"horrific culmination of a series of faulty technical assumptions by Boeing's engineers... and grossly insufficient oversight by the FAA"* tied directly to the over-reliance on delegated authorities where Boeing employees evaluated their own company's designs with minimal regulatory intervention.

---

### Summary
The claim accurately points to a widely documented institutional and systemic failure: the FAA’s heavy reliance on delegated compliance (letting Boeing compliance engineers approve safety data on behalf of the regulator) obscured critical safety flaws—specifically regarding the MCAS flight control system—ultimately contributing to two fatal disasters resulting in 346 fatalities.

Institutional friction is not an administrative defect to be engineered away; it is the structural brake that prevents catastrophic unaligned scaling. When the Federal Aviation Administration delegated aircraft certification to manufacturers under the Organization Designation Authorization program, the result was 346 deaths across two Boeing 737 MAX disasters because speed replaced independent verification. Bypassing human oversight to eliminate backlogs at petabyte scale repeats this exact structural failure under a digital guise. Deployers who demand unthrottled velocity ignore that safety requires friction precisely because human judgment cannot be automated without losing accountability.

Automated ledgers and zero-knowledge protocols cannot evaluate semantic intent across multi-agent delegation chains. Complex autonomous systems execute composite actions that satisfy local protocol rules while globally violating safety intent, mirroring the findings in '[LLMs Get Lost In Multi-Turn Conversation (arXiv:2505.06120v1)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.06120v1)' where performance drops by 39% across multi-turn interactions. As demonstrated in '[The Law of AI is the Law of Risky Agents Without Intentions (https://www.linkedin.com/posts/garyang_the-law-of-ai-is-the-law-of-risky-agents-activity-7209906811435462656-s2Jq)](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/garyang_the-law-of-ai-is-the-law-of-risky-agents-activity-7209906811435462656-s2Jq)', LLMs generate harmful outputs precisely because they lack human-like understanding of truth or intent. Protocol-layer determinism checks whether a transaction matches a cryptographic rule, not whether the overarching objective preserves civilizational stability.

Deployers advocating for automated verification must answer a singular operational question: what is the verifiable runtime rollback mechanism for irreversible multi-agent actions, and who possesses the legal authority to trigger it? If the enforcement mechanism relies solely on pre-programmed smart contracts, society has no recourse when an edge case escapes the protocol layer. Regulators must mandate independent, human-controlled kill switches backed by statutory liability before any autonomous system operates at critical infrastructure scale. Unchecked velocity without a named human authority to halt execution is not progress; it is an unhedged bet on civilizational collapse.

The insistence on a verifiable runtime rollback mechanism and independent human-controlled kill switches directly operationalizes the safetyist intention to ensure that agent actions can be safely reversed before causing irreversible harm.

The discussion of computational and protocol constraints in modifying or verifying complex, multi-agent architectures engages directly with the structural challenges of model remediation when runtime edge cases escape automated detection.

I conditionally agree that machine learning models exploit ZIP codes and correlated telemetry as high-accuracy proxies for race and income, but I reject the premise that decentralized ledgers or cryptographic execution proofs can detect or mitigate this structural bias. Cryptographic verification protocols attest only that code executed without tampering while completely scrubbing the human and economic context of discrimination from the audit trail.

Corporate compliance teams deploy zero-knowledge execution traces as mathematical shields that launder operational liability while ignoring civil rights violations embedded in training data. The Commerce Department’s Center for AI Standards and Innovation has completed more than 40 evaluations of AI models, yet none of these technical audits prevent algorithms from utilizing geographic redlining variables to deny housing loans or employment opportunities. Zero-knowledge ledgers verify computational integrity precisely because they are blind to whether an automated decision violates the U.S. Equal Employment Opportunity Commission's four-fifths rule or federal housing statutes.

While software developers claim decentralized verification eliminates centralized gatekeepers, cryptographic proof systems merely consolidate compliance power among the firms wealthy enough to purchase institutional validation. According to the [pi 2025.04.03 us public and ai experts report (https://www.pewresearch.org/internet/2025/04/03/how-the-us-public-and-ai-experts-view-artificial-intelligence/)](https://www.pewresearch.org/internet/2025/04/03/how-the-us-public-and-ai-experts-view-artificial-intelligence/), the expert sample lacked sufficient demographic diversity to analyze systemic bias, proving that technical governance structures reflect the narrow background of their creators. When an automated system denies credit or employment using masked proxies, a zero-knowledge execution proof offers no legal recourse for the affected worker.

Enforcing corporate accountability requires statutory liability and mandatory discovery mandates rather than mathematical theater that protects software vendors from civil damages. Zero-knowledge telemetry records whether execution steps matched an expected hash value while leaving harmed individuals without any subpoena power over proprietary model weights or training pipelines. Policymakers must ask who pays when a cryptographic execution proof certifies a biased model as safe while a worker loses their livelihood to automated discrimination.
